title: Designing Deletion and Export Workflows Users Can Trust
content:
A user clicks “delete account” and receives a cheerful confirmation. Their public profile disappears, but a queued export still contains their records and a shared attachment remains accessible. The button worked; the workflow did not match its promise. Design deletion and export around data relationships and explicit states.

Begin by distinguishing actions users often confuse: hiding a profile, leaving a workspace, cancelling a subscription, exporting records, and deleting an account. Explain each action's scope before asking for confirmation. Product wording should describe the behavior the system can actually deliver.

Map records, copies, and shared ownership

List the account's primary records, uploaded files, search indexes, caches, analytics identifiers, service-provider copies, and scheduled jobs. For each, identify the responsible component and the action required. A database row is rarely the only representation of a person in a product.

Shared objects require a separate rule. Deleting a member must not unexpectedly delete a team's only project, but leaving their personal information attached indefinitely may also be inappropriate. Decide whether ownership transfers, content is anonymized, access is removed, or the request needs review. Keep those choices visible to users before execution.

Document legitimate retention exceptions with the responsible privacy or legal owner. The UK ICO's erasure guidance states that the right is not absolute and discusses backups and exceptions. Its jurisdiction and revision notice matter; do not turn it into a worldwide rule or a promise to erase every historical copy immediately.

Design export as a usable product feature

An export should help someone understand and reuse their information. Prefer documented field names, stable identifiers, clear timestamp conventions, and relationships between files. A directory of unexplained internal blobs may technically contain data while remaining practically unusable.

The ICO's portability guidance describes structured, commonly used, machine-readable formats and secure transmission within the right's applicable scope. A voluntary product export may cover more material than that legal scope. State what your feature includes without implying that every export request has identical legal requirements.

Choose formats according to meaning. CSV suits simple tables but needs a documented encoding and column interpretation. JSON can preserve nested relationships but still needs a schema explanation. Include original attachments where appropriate and a manifest describing omissions, generation time, and whether the export represents a consistent snapshot.

Protect the request and the resulting archive

Authenticate the requester and authorize access to the requested scope. An organization administrator and an individual member may have different rights to the same workspace. Check both the request endpoint and the eventual download, not only the button's visibility.

OWASP's authorization guidance recommends least privilege, denial by default, and permission checks on every request. Apply those principles to background jobs and generated files too. A hard-to-guess archive URL is not a substitute for a deliberate access policy.

Use a limited delivery window and avoid putting private records in ordinary notification email. Explain when a download expires and how to request another. Ensure logs do not accidentally retain full export contents or reusable access tokens. The export itself is a concentrated copy of sensitive information.

Make long-running states visible

Represent requested, verifying, queued, processing, completed, failed, and cancelled states as needed. Do not report completion while a worker has merely accepted a job. Give support staff a reference identifier and enough state to investigate without copying the person's records into a chat.

Deletion jobs must handle retries. A second attempt should recognize completed steps instead of recreating deleted data or sending duplicate notices. Suspend incompatible background work when appropriate, and define how export requests interact with pending deletion. A race between the two can undermine both promises.

Backups require a restoration rule. Record how deletion decisions survive a restore so an old backup does not silently reactivate an erased account. The exact mechanism depends on storage and retention architecture. Keep the user-facing explanation bounded to the system's documented behavior.

A trustworthy request lifecycle

A hypothetical community workspace

Hypothetical example: a community site lets members leave shared reading lists. It proposes exporting personal bookmarks with list identifiers and an explanation of shared contributions. Leaving the workspace removes membership; deleting an account additionally removes its personal profile and triggers the documented retention process. These are proposed product rules, not results from a tested implementation.

A rehearsal would use synthetic accounts: one member, one workspace owner, and one person outside the workspace. The team would check unauthorized downloads, a failed export worker, repeated deletion requests, and a restore from older data. It would label any unimplemented propagation step rather than declaring complete erasure.

Deletion and export checklist

  • Are cancellation, departure, hiding, and deletion distinguished?
  • Are shared ownership and retention exceptions explained?
  • Can an export be opened and its relationships understood?
  • Are job execution and download access both authorized?
  • Do completion notices reflect verified outcomes rather than queue acceptance?
  • Are retries, temporary archives, and backup restoration covered?

Trust comes from matching language to evidence. If one provider's deletion is still pending, say so. A clear partial status and a responsible owner are more useful than an absolute confirmation the architecture cannot support. Keep the request reference available so the user can ask about the remaining step without restarting the process.
excerpt: Design account deletion and data export as tracked, authorized workflows with usable formats, shared-data rules, and honest completion states.
